facts.statement: Chaoyangia beishanensis was discovered in the Jiufotang Formation near Chaoyang in Liaoning province, China.
facts.quote: The specimen (museum catalog number IVPP V9934) was discovered in the Jiufotang Formation near the city of Chaoyang in Liaoning province, China.

facts.statement: Chaoyangia lived during the Aptian age of the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 120 million years ago.
facts.quote: This rock formation has been dated to the Aptian age of the Early Cretaceous period, 120 million years ago.

facts.statement: Chaoyangia is known from a single partial skeleton that includes vertebrae, ribs, hips, and upper legs.
facts.quote: This species is known from a single fossil specimen consisting of a partial skeleton including vertebra, ribs, hips, and upper legs.

facts.statement: The species was originally placed in its own order, Chaoyangiformes, by its describer Hou.
facts.quote: Hou, who recognized the species as a euornithean, also placed it in its own order, Chaoyangiformes.

facts.statement: A 2012 study confirmed that Chaoyangia is a primitive euornithean (ornithuran) based on phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: In 2012, paleontologists Jingmai O'Connor and Zhou Zhong re-described the original Chaoyangia specimen, and confirmed that it was indeed a primitive euornithean (=ornithuran) using a phylogenetic analysis.

facts.statement: Some researchers have debated whether Chaoyangia and Songlingornis are synonyms after Songlingornis was removed from the genus.
facts.quote: The removal of this specimen from Chaoyangia left its identity uncertain, and some researchers continued to suspect Songlingornis and Chaoyangia were synonyms.

facts.statement: Chaoyangia is classified within the parent group Ornithuromorpha.

rejected.statement: Chaoyangia were small birds characterized by more than eight fused sacral vertebrae, long angled rib processes, and a distinct neck in the femur.
rejected.quote: Chaoyangia were small, basal euornithean birds characterized by more than eight fused sacral vertebrae (those connected to the hips), uniquely long, slender, and angled uncinate processes on the ribs, and a distinct 'neck' in the upper leg bone (femur).
